A quantitative research programme · the one positive result

The Edge That Held

Direction is a mirage — except for one signal that keeps working: cross-sectional momentum. We found it by accident while trying to kill trend lines, then subjected it to the test that should have debunked it. It survived.

12-1 momentum · UK equities · survivorship-free · net of costs

How we got here

Every attempt to trade on chart geometry failed — support/resistance breakouts, rising-channel timing, buy-the-dip, ride-the-winner, capital rotation. All lost to buy-and-hold, robustly. But one variant looked promising: holding the names that were in strong rising channels. On inspection, that wasn't a trend-line effect at all — it was cross-sectional momentum in disguise. So we isolated it and tested it properly.

Momentum is a ranked-return signal, not a chart pattern: rank stocks by their return over the past 12 months skipping the most recent one (the "12-1"), hold the winners, rebalance monthly. You don't need lines to capture it — and the line-drawing machinery, it turned out, only got in the way.

The test that should have killed it

Survivorship: the alpha survived

Our first momentum backtest used current FTSE constituents — a survivor-only universe that flatters momentum more than almost any factor, because the losers it would have avoided are simply missing. So we bought a genuine survivorship-free universe: 3,237 UK stocks — 1,570 live and 1,667 delisted (Carillion, Thomas Cook, NMC…), full history. The worry was that the edge would evaporate. It didn't.

Survivorship bias inflated the market benchmark (~3pp/yr) more than it inflated momentum — which already avoids losers. So the alpha held, and was marginally higher survivorship-free. And the market-neutral book improved (Sharpe 0.25 → 0.65), because shorting the delisted losers — absent from the survivor set — actually pays.

Is it tradeable?

The constraint is drawdown, not cost

The tilt trades slowly — about 6.3× one-way turnover a year — so the bid/offer spread barely touches it: net of a liquidity-tiered spread (15/40/80 bps), the long-only tilt earns 10.6% CAGR at Sharpe 0.72 versus the market's 5.65% / 0.42. The biggest friction is actually UK stamp duty — 0.5% on every purchase, ~1.2pp/yr, larger than the spread — which takes the tilt to ~9.0% / 0.63 on a taxable share account. Even so the edge dwarfs it, and it is avoided entirely inside an ISA or SIPP.

Even net of spread and stamp duty the strategy clears the market by a wide margin, and the break-even spread is ~200 bps — an order of magnitude above realistic execution (spread + stamp ≈ 65 bps on a liquid-tier buy). Monthly rebalancing still beats quarterly (Sharpe 0.72 vs 0.63): the turnover saving isn't worth the responsiveness lost, because cost was never the binding constraint — drawdown is.

The cost of admission is drawdown, not cost

The long-only tilt is a high-beta long book (β ≈ 0.84), so its worst months are simply market crashes — −20% in 2008, −17% in the 2020 COVID crash — and its max drawdown is ~−47%. The market-neutral version removes the beta but exposes the momentum crash: a −48% single month in April 2009 and a −64% max drawdown. Real, but a brutal tail to hold or lever.

Improving the build

Two levers, pulling different axes

If the binding constraint is drawdown rather than cost, there are two independent things to try: shrink the drawdown, and lift the return per unit of it. One is a position-sizing trick; the other adds orthogonal information. They turn out not to fight.

Vol-targeting — the drawdown lever

Scale exposure inversely to the tilt's own recent volatility (causal 12-month estimate): lean in when it's calm, step back when it's wild. With no leverage this cuts the max drawdown from −47% to −38% at essentially no return cost (CAGR 10.6% → 10.3%), and nudges Sharpe up (0.72 → 0.76). Real risk control, modest — position sizing can't manufacture return.

Quality, value and low-volatility — the return lever

Overlay cross-sectional factors and rank names on the blend. Quality (ROE + gross-profitability) and value (earnings- and book-yield) come from point-in-time fundamentals — each figure dated to when it was actually filed, so the backtest never peeks. Low-volatility (prefer calmer names) needs only price history. Blend with momentum, hold the top quintile.

Factor overlay on the tilt (survivorship-free top-350, net of spread)

value alone12.86%0.74−61%

Quality and low-volatility are momentum's natural partners. Quality lifts Sharpe 0.72 → 0.80 at the same drawdown; adding low-vol lifts it again to 0.85 — both are defensive, both currency-neutral, both fully covered. Value is greedier: the highest standalone return (12.86%) but a brutal −61% drawdown, and it needs a wide book to help — so it's an optional return-chaser, not the default. We also tested a low-vol level against vol change (a regime-shift idea): change consistently hurt, so only the level is used.

Where the levers meet

The best build

Because the levers act on different axes — return versus drawdown — they stack. Vol-target the quality- and low-vol-tilted book and you get momentum's best partners and its drawdown control at once. And because low-vol and vol-targeting are both volatility-aware, they compound.

From plain momentum to the recommended build (net of spread)

+ vol-target (lev ≤ 1.5)13.81%0.90−43%

The recommended build is momentum tilted by quality and low-volatility, vol-targeted, unlevered: 11.2% / Sharpe 0.89 / −40% net of spread (≈ 10.1% / 0.81 after stamp duty on a taxable account). Versus plain momentum that's more return, a big Sharpe jump (0.72 → 0.89), and ~7pp less drawdown — all at once, with no borrowing.

Leverage is nearly free here. Allowing up to 1.5× lifts CAGR from 11.2% to 13.8% — a full extra ~2.5pp a year — while the drawdown only widens from −40% to −43% and Sharpe holds (0.89 → 0.90). That's the most efficient point on the frontier; the same leverage on a value-heavy book buys return far more expensively (deeper drawdown).

Not a month-end fluke

Every rebalance in this study lands on a month-end — so we checked it isn't the reason it works. Shifting the entire monthly cycle across the calendar, so the strategy starts on a different day of the month, leaves the edge intact: across ten calendar phases the momentum tilt beats the market in all ten (mean edge +4.6pp a year) and the factor-tilted book in all ten too (+5.4pp), with CAGR clustered at 10–11%. You would have beaten the market starting on any day.

How to actually run it

Living with the drawdown

The mechanics decide what to hold; the discipline decides whether you actually capture the edge — because the ways this strategy fails are behavioural, not analytical.

Stay unlevered

Leverage is a mirage here: it lifted return but not Sharpe (0.89 → 0.90) — amplification, not alpha — and the backtest never charged the borrowing. Worse, it introduces the one risk a backtest can't show: a margin call that forces you to sell at the bottom, turning a paper drawdown into a permanent loss and knocking you out of the recovery. Staying unlevered is exactly what preserves your ability to hold — which is the whole game.

The drawdown is the price, not a flaw

You're paid the ~6%/yr because you sit through −40% drawdowns most people can't — if it were comfortable it would be arbitraged away. So decide the rules while calm: hold it as long-horizon money, sized so a worse-than-backtest fall (say −60%, held for years) cannot force you to sell, and treat only the strategy misbehaving versus its design — never the pain — as a reason to stop. Depth of drawdown is not the signal; healthy strategies have deep ones.

Fund it with regular contributions — for the right reasons

Feeding the position with steady, pre-committed contributions is the disciplined form of "buy more when it's cheap" — but we tested it, and the dip-buying bonus isn't real: averaging into the volatile build slightly underperformed the same money into a smooth asset of equal return, and the effect fades to nothing as the pot grows (a fixed contribution is 3% of the pot at year 2, under 1% by year 5). What contributions genuinely give: the optimal way to deploy income, a cushioned experienced drawdown (the portfolio value fell ~−30% under a monthly drip versus −40% on invested capital, because inflows soften the fall), and — most valuable — they take the human out of the loop, so you keep buying through the fear.

If you keep a reserve for the dips, release it by rule. When the strategy is deep in drawdown, check the market: if the market is also down, it's cheap equity beta that has always recovered — add a pre-set tranche. If the strategy fell while the market didn't, that's a momentum-specific problem — freeze and investigate, don't add. Historically all seven of the strategy's drawdowns were the market-driven kind (in the 2008 crash it fell −40% against the market's −53%). The reserve must be bounded and pre-committed — open-ended "add more as it falls" is a martingale and a route to ruin.

What we won't claim

Honest caveats

It's a high-beta tilt with real alpha, not market-neutral magic — most of the 10.6% is equity beta; the value-add over that is ~+6%/yr. The survivorship-free universe is messy (bad ticks in delisted micro-caps), so returns are winsorised cross-sectionally — a cleaning judgment the exact numbers depend on, though the liquid top-350 is relatively clean. The value factor is thin (currency-restricted to ~1,300 names) — which is why the build uses quality and low-volatility, both currency-neutral and fully covered, rather than value. On a UK taxable share account, stamp duty costs ~1.2pp/yr (bigger than the spread) — real, though sheltered inside an ISA/SIPP. Vol-targeting tames the drawdown (−47% → −40%) but doesn't abolish it — a real edge is not an easy one, and you still sit through deep, beta-driven drops to earn it. Results are one market (UK), one construction.

Where it sits in the programme

Direction is a mirage no chart pattern beats. The one exception is momentum — winners keep winning over a year — and it is captured by ranking returns, not by drawing lines.

Across a dozen experiments, every repeatable edge was a risk-premium-shaped thing — sell insurance, bear a crash, collect a modest, honest return. Momentum is the directional member of that family: a real, survivorship-robust, cost-robust premium whose price is a fat left tail. It is the programme's standout positive result — and, fittingly, the one idea that owes nothing to the trend lines that led us to it.

Provenance

12-1 cross-sectional momentum (12-month return skipping the most recent month), monthly rebalance, top-quintile long-only tilt and top-minus-bottom market-neutral book. Universe: 3,237 GBP/GBX LSE common stocks (1,570 live + 1,667 delisted) from EODHD, full OHLCV; point-in-time top-350 by liquidity. Returns winsorised cross-sectionally (1/99). Costs: liquidity-tiered spread (15/40/80 bps round-trip) applied on turnover, plus 0.5% UK stamp duty on purchases for a taxable share account (~1.2pp/yr, the largest friction); break-even and sensitivity reported. Backtest 2001–2026, net, with year-block bootstrap CI [+4.2%, +19.5%] on the long-only annual mean. Calendar-phase robustness tested by shifting the whole monthly cycle 0–27 days (the index-shift preserves delisting, which a naïve forward-fill would not): the edge holds in all ten phases. Recommended build tilts momentum by quality and low-volatility, then vol-targets exposure to a constant volatility from a causal 12-month estimate. Factors: quality = ½·ROE + ½·gross-profitability and low-volatility = −trailing 12-month return vol (both currency-neutral); value = ½·book-yield + ½·earnings-yield (currency-aligned names only, from point-in-time fundamentals dated to each statement's filing date). The 12-1 window, universe size, holding count and a vol-change factor were all sweep-tested; 12-1, ~350 names and the top quintile hold up, vol-change does not. Scripts and full results in trend-channel-experiment/ and the implementation spec in MOMENTUM_STRATEGY_SPEC.md; data in data/eodhd/ (local-only). A validated research programme, honestly caveated — not investment advice.
